# Scope

This guide follows the public lessons retrieved from the [Linear Algebra playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLBh2i93oe2quLc5zaxD0WHzQTGrXMwAI6). Members-only and unavailable lessons are excluded.

# Unit 1 — Foundations of vector spaces

Videos: 1, 2, 4, 5.

Vectors in \(\mathbb R^n\) are tuples of scalars. A line through a point \(\mathbf p\) with direction \(\mathbf v\) is

$$
L=\{\mathbf p+t\mathbf v:t\in\mathbb R\}.
$$

A vector space is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication and satisfies the vector-space axioms. A subspace \(U\subseteq V\) must contain \(0\) and satisfy

$$
\mathbf u,\mathbf v\in U,\ a,b\in\mathbb R
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v\in U.
$$

Representative problem: determine whether the solution set of \(x+2y-z=0\) is a subspace of \(\mathbb R^3\), and parameterize it.

# Unit 2 — Subspaces, inner products, and geometry

Videos: 6, 9, 10.

The Euclidean inner product and norm are

$$
\langle\mathbf u,\mathbf v\rangle=\sum_i u_iv_i,
\qquad
\|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{\langle\mathbf v,\mathbf v\rangle}.
$$

The angle relation is

$$
\langle\mathbf u,\mathbf v\rangle=\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta.
$$

In \(\mathbb R^3\), \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\) is perpendicular to both inputs and has magnitude equal to the parallelogram area:

$$
\|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|=\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|\sin\theta.
$$

Representative problem: compute the projection of \(\mathbf u\) onto nonzero \(\mathbf v\):

$$
\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf v}(\mathbf u)=
\frac{\langle\mathbf u,\mathbf v\rangle}{\langle\mathbf v,\mathbf v\rangle}\mathbf v.
$$

# Unit 3 — Matrices and linear maps

Videos: 11, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20.

A linear map satisfies

$$
T(a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v)=aT(\mathbf u)+bT(\mathbf v).
$$

For a matrix \(A=[\mathbf a_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf a_n]\),

$$
A\mathbf x=x_1\mathbf a_1+\cdots+x_n\mathbf a_n.
$$

Composition is matrix multiplication:

$$
(AB)\mathbf x=A(B\mathbf x).
$$

The matrix of a linear map is determined by the images of the standard basis vectors. Special matrices include diagonal, triangular, symmetric, and identity matrices.

Representative problem: find the matrix of \(T(x,y)=(2x-y,x+3y)\), then compute \(T(1,2)\).

# Unit 4 — Independence, bases, coordinates, and dimension

Videos: 22, 23, 25, 26, 28.

Vectors \(\mathbf v_1,\ldots,\mathbf v_k\) are linearly independent when

$$
c_1\mathbf v_1+\cdots+c_k\mathbf v_k=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
c_1=\cdots=c_k=0.
$$

A basis is an independent spanning set. Coordinates relative to a basis \(B=(\mathbf b_1,\ldots,\mathbf b_n)\) satisfy

$$
\mathbf v=[\mathbf v]_B{}_1\mathbf b_1+\cdots+[\mathbf v]_B{}_n\mathbf b_n.
$$

The exchange lemma explains why all bases of a finite-dimensional space have the same number of vectors: the dimension.

Representative problem: express \((5,1)\) in the basis \(\{(1,1),(2,-1)\}\).

# Unit 5 — Inverses and transposes

Videos: 29, 31, 32.

An inverse satisfies

$$
AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I.
$$

For a \(2\times2\) matrix,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}^{-1}
=\frac1{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix},
\qquad ad-bc\ne0.
$$

The transpose is defined by

$$
(A^T)_{ij}=A_{ji},
\qquad (AB)^T=B^TA^T.
$$

Representative problem: find the inverse of \(\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\) and verify it by multiplication.

# Unit 6 — Range, kernel, rank-nullity, and solving systems

Videos: 34, 35, 37, 38, 40, 42.

The kernel and range are

$$
\ker(A)=\{\mathbf x:A\mathbf x=0\},
\qquad
\operatorname{range}(A)=\{A\mathbf x:\mathbf x\in V\}.
$$

The rank-nullity theorem is

$$
\dim(V)=\operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{nullity}(A).
$$

Row operations preserve the solution set of a system when applied to its augmented matrix. In row-echelon form, pivot variables are determined and free variables parameterize the remaining solutions.

Representative problem: row-reduce an augmented matrix and state whether the system has no solution, one solution, or infinitely many solutions.

# Unit 7 — Determinants

Videos: 43, 44, 46, 47, 48, 50, 51.

For a \(2\times2\) matrix,

$$
\det\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}=ad-bc.
$$

The determinant is multilinear and alternating, and satisfies

$$
\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).
$$

For an \(n\times n\) matrix, Laplace expansion along row \(i\) is

$$
\det(A)=\sum_j(-1)^{i+j}a_{ij}\det(A_{ij}).
$$

Geometrically, \(|\det(A)|\) is volume scaling. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

Representative problem: compute the determinant of \(\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\0&4&5\\1&0&6\end{bmatrix}\) by expansion or elimination.

# Unit 8 — Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

Videos: 53, 54, 55.

An eigenvector is a nonzero vector satisfying

$$
A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v.
$$

Eigenvalues solve the characteristic equation

$$
p_A(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
$$

The algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue is its multiplicity as a root of \(p_A\). Eigenvectors for \(\lambda\) form the eigenspace

$$
E_\lambda=\ker(A-\lambda I).
$$

Representative problem: find the eigenvalues and eigenspaces of \(\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\).

# Quiz

Attempt this closed-notes. Each question is worth 2 points.

1. Parameterize the line through \((1,2)\) parallel to \((3,-1)\).
2. Prove that the solution set of a homogeneous linear system is a subspace.
3. Compute \(\langle(1,2,-1),(2,0,3)\rangle\) and both vector norms.
4. Compute \((1,2,0)\times(2,-1,1)\).
5. Find the matrix of \(T(x,y)=(2x-y,x+3y)\).
6. Explain why the columns of a matrix determine its matrix-vector product.
7. Test whether \((1,2)\) and \((2,4)\) are linearly independent.
8. Find the coordinates of \((5,1)\) in the basis \(\{(1,1),(2,-1)\}\).
9. Find the inverse of \(\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\).
10. State and interpret the rank-nullity theorem.
11. Describe how free variables appear in a row-echelon solution.
12. Compute \(\det\begin{bmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}\).
13. State the determinant criterion for invertibility.
14. Find the characteristic polynomial of \(\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\).
15. Find the eigenspaces of that matrix.
16. Explain why eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.

## Scoring

- 28–32: ready for proof-heavy linear algebra.
- 20–27: review the units containing missed questions.
- Below 20: revisit Units 1, 3, 4, and 6 before continuing.

See the [answer key](answer.qmd) after attempting the quiz.
